# RHO: Your Coding Agent is Secretly a Roboticist

> Anonymous project page for a paper under double-anonymous review.

- **Authors**: Anonymous

---

## Abstract

Code-as-Policies (CaP) has shown that large language models can write code to solve robotics tasks by composing perception, planning, and control primitives. Recent CaP systems, however, rely on multi-turn code-generation loops at test time, which is often infeasible for real-time robot control.

We introduce **Robotics Harness Optimization (RHO)**, a paradigm in which tool-enabled coding agents, *at training time*, propose and search for interpretable neurosymbolic multi-file policy repositories (*Repositories-as-Policies*) that compose these primitives rather than a single prompt, function, or file. RHO searches with reflective feedback from environment reward and execution rather than demonstrations.

Our method generalizes to perturbed pick-and-place settings like LIBERO-PRO, reaching 64.33% success where CaP-Agent0, the prior leader, reaches 18.03% over the same primitive API, and where VLAs trained from demonstrations, π0.5 and OpenVLA, average 13.20% and 0.0%. Under single-turn evaluation on Robosuite, RHO reaches 70.0% at 9.31 s per trial, exceeding the 68.29% prior record that required up to six turns of corrective code edits and 113.6 s per trial, a 12.20× speedup.

The evolved repository deploys unchanged to a different robot from the one simulated, and picks up objects never seen during training in 17 of 20 real trials. When an LLM is used in the control loop, as on RAI’s hard O3DE benchmark, RHO optimizes the deployed agent’s multi-file harness of prompts, tools, and control code, improving held-out success from 23.5% to 44.3% with 20% less wall-clock time and 27% fewer tool calls.

## Method

### How CaP methods buy success today

A Code-as-Policies agent raises its success rate at test time: it generates several programs per turn, merges them, asks a vision-language model whether the scene changed as intended, and runs the turn again. RHO pays that cost once during optimization and ships frozen code.

## Results

## Demos

Each trial is shown at 1× speed. The arm's speed is not a variable we expose to RHO and can be tuned for faster deployments. 20 trials were run: 17 success and 3 failures. We display a subset.

### Kinova Gen3 with Robotiq gripper

Three things change between simulation and these trials.

 
 1
 A new object
 The search ran on cubes. Deployment lifts a computer mouse, absent from simulation.
 
 
 2
 A moved position
 A hand re-places the mouse between trials, and in one case while the policy is running.
 
 
 3
 A different embodiment
 Simulation ran on a Franka Panda. These trials run on a Kinova Gen3.
 

### Reading the failure

The arm descends three times onto the spot the mouse left. Grasp synthesis falls back to a path that places the grasp at the median of a segmentation mask's deprojected depth points, with orientation from a fixed top-down set. Those fall-back attempts stay anchored to the initial observation, so every retry targets a stale pose.

We found this by watching the trial, reading the logs and walking the code. Auditing the same logic inside an end-to-end policy remains an open problem in interpretability. The fix is twelve lines in this repository, with no retraining and no new demonstrations. The trials above ran without it.

## Hardware

### Primitives

CaP-Bench exposes each stage separately. RAI covers grasp planning, inverse kinematics and execution in `move_to_point`. At the time of submission, RAI’s manipulation demo exposes five tools. We intentionally expose only three to the agent in the O3DE experiments with the tool names and signatures fixed. RHO’s search process remains fixed across any set of primitives. It searches for the best *Repositories-as-Policies* that compose these primitives to maximize the user provided score.

### Simulation

| | CaP-Bench, Robosuite | RAI, O3DE |
|---|---|---|
| Platform | Dual-socket server | AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 workstation |
| CPU | 2 × Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 | 16 Zen 5 cores |
| GPU | 2 × NVIDIA B200 | Radeon 8060S, 40 RDNA 3.5 CUs,
128 GB unified memory |

The RAI experiments ran entirely on the one workstation: ROS 2, MoveIt, O3DE with Vulkan rendering, the perception models, and the coding agent.

### Robots

| | Franka Emika Panda | Kinova Gen3 |
|---|---|---|
| Gripper | Franka Hand | Robotiq 2F-85 |
| Colour camera | Intel RealSense D435i | Omnivision OV5640 |
| Depth camera | Intel RealSense D435i | Intel RealSense D410 |
| Colour resolution | 640 × 480 | 1280 × 720 |
| Camera location | External | Wrist-mounted |
| Tasks | Lift Cube — 14/20 | Lift Mouse — 17/20 |
| | Stack Cube — 11/20 | |

The Kinova’s camera sits on the wrist, close to the object. The Franka’s is external and much further back, with a third of the pixels. In the vast majority of trials, Contact-GraspNet fails to produce graspable points and the programs fall back to fixed grasp poses. The grasp synthesis depends on mask quality, so the Franka working from a coarser view (several meters vs under one meter) has a much more challenging deployment environment. This is why Lift Mouse on the Kinova succeeds more often than the nominally simpler Lift Cube on the Franka.
